title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

reading.body:
An attorney used a generative AI system to create case citations for a legal brief, submitting two entirely fabricated court cases and a false quotation from a real case to support arguments in a civil suit. The failure occurred at the point of submission to the court, where no human review caught that the cases did not exist before the opposing attorney exposed them during a hearing. This would have been prevented by basic verification of citations against legal databases, a standard step that the use of AI output should have prompted rather than replaced.

The AI system itself performed as such systems typically do when asked to generate citations, producing plausible-looking but false legal authority. The deployment failure was the attorney's decision to file the output without verification, treating generated text as a source rather than as a draft requiring fact-checking. Whether the attorney understood he was relying on fabrications is not established by the reporting.

reports.title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

summary:
Minnesota attorney Faisal S. Ahmed has been suspended for 30 days after submitting fake court cases generated by artificial intelligence in a 2025 legal brief. Ahmed, licensed since 2014, cited two nonexistent cases, Anderson v. City of Biwabik and Doherty v. Alma E. Clark Memorial Home, in a Hennepin County civil suit involving a Robbinsdale food store owner being sued for unpaid rent. He also included a false quotation from a real case and made citation errors. The opposing attorney discovered the fabrications during an August hearing.

Judge Lois Conroy ruled against Ahmed's client, ordering payment of $233,563 in back rent, and fined Ahmed $5,000. She referred him to the Minnesota Lawyer's Professional Responsibility Board. Ahmed agreed to the 30-day suspension and must pay an additional $900 in costs. This case is part of a growing pattern, with over 800 documented instances of litigants using AI to create fake legal citations. The Minnesota Supreme Court has reminded attorneys that ethical obligations apply to all use of artificial intelligence tools.
